extracted.intended_audience: researchers, policy-makers, and funders concerned with peer-review fairness and grant-review processes
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluation rubric used by the Swedish Medical Research Council for postdoctoral fellowship applications: reviewers scored applicants on three dimensions (scientific competence, methodological quality, relevance) with each criterion rated 0–4 and summed to produce an overall ranking. The paper analyzes bias in those scores using objective productivity benchmarks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific competence of the applicant
rubrics_metrics.description: One of three reviewer-scored criteria; intended to measure the applicant's scientific ability/track record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scored 0–4. Wennerås & Wold find this criterion is systematically biased by gender: female applicants received lower competence scores than males of equivalent measurable productivity (a woman needed ~2.5× productivity to receive the same competence score as a man).

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality of the proposed methodology
rubrics_metrics.description: One of three reviewer-scored criteria; intended to assess the methodological rigor and soundness of the proposed work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scored 0–4 and summed with other criteria to produce overall ranking. Paper does not detail rubric sub-items for method quality but treats it as one of the three numeric dimensions used for ranking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relevance of the research proposal
rubrics_metrics.description: One of three reviewer-scored criteria; intended to assess the scientific relevance/importance of the proposed research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scored 0–4 and summed with other criteria to produce overall ranking. No finer-grained scoring guidance provided in the paper beyond the 0–4 scale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scoring scale and aggregation (0–4 per criterion, summed)
rubrics_metrics.description: Each of the three criteria was scored on a 0–4 scale and the three scores were summed to form an overall ranking for applicants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used by the funder to rank fellowship applicants. Findings in the paper analyze how these numeric scores relate to objective productivity measures and to applicant gender and affiliations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Total publications (productivity benchmark)
rubrics_metrics.description: Objective measure used by the authors to operationalize applicant productivity: the total number of publications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treated as one of the strongest objective predictors of reviewers' competence scores in statistical models.

rubrics_metrics.name: First-author publications (productivity benchmark)
rubrics_metrics.description: Objective measure used by the authors: count of first-author papers as an indicator of independent productivity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Included in models and identified as a strong objective predictor of competence scores.

rubrics_metrics.name: Total impact-factor-weighted publications (productivity benchmark)
rubrics_metrics.description: Productivity metric summing publication counts weighted by the journals' impact factors (total impact points).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One of the strongest predictors of competence scores; used by the authors as an objective truth-reference. The paper quantifies nepotism effects in terms of impact-points (e.g., affiliation effect comparable to ~100 impact-points).

rubrics_metrics.name: Citations (productivity benchmark)
rubrics_metrics.description: Total citations to the applicant's work used as an objective measure of research impact/productivity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Included as a predictor of competence scores; among the objective metrics the authors used to compare against subjective reviewer judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Educational level / years post-degree (productivity/capacity benchmark)
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicant's formal educational attainment and time since degree used as control/benchmark variables in analyses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treated as part of the objective covariates to explain reviewer scores; included alongside publications/citations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gender bias magnitude (empirical finding relevant to rubric validity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical result: female applicants received systematically lower competence scores than equally productive male applicants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quantified effect: a woman needed approximately 2.5 times the measured productivity (by the authors' composite benchmarks) to obtain the same competence score as a man. Demonstrates that an investigator/competence criterion can capture rater stereotypes rather than objective merit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affiliation / nepotism effect (empirical finding)
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants affiliated with a member of the review committee received higher scores than non-affiliates of equivalent productivity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quantified effect: affiliation increased scores by about 0.5 points on the 4-point scale; the magnitude was comparable to having an extra ~100 impact-points of publications. Shows that social/organizational ties distort numeric scoring.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combined effect of gender and affiliation
rubrics_metrics.description: Interactional empirical finding: gender and affiliation together produced the largest differences in outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Being female AND non-affiliated produced the worst outcomes in scores, while being male AND affiliated produced the best outcomes—effects largely independent of measurable productivity, indicating multiplicative disadvantages/advantages in the reviewed rubric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implication: vulnerability of 'competence/investigator' criteria to stereotype capture
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors' implication for rubric design: criteria labeled as 'competence' or assessing the investigator are susceptible to reflecting reviewers' stereotypes rather than objective productivity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wennerås & Wold recommend caution in using vague investigator/competence criteria without objective benchmarks; their productivity benchmarks became a template for subsequent fairness audits and suggest that rubric designers should include objective, transparent measures to reduce stereotype-driven variance.
